title: UNIT 7: STATISTICS
notes:
✓ Statistics → the branch of mathematics concerned with collecting, organizing, presenting, analyzing and interpreting data.

◆ Data → information collected for a purpose.

→ Statistics helps us summarize large amounts of information and make decisions from data.

title: 7.1 TYPES OF DATA
notes:
Data can be classified according to the nature of the information and how values are obtained.

✓ Qualitative data → describes qualities or categories rather than numerical measurements.

Examples → gender, colour, occupation, type of vehicle.

✓ Quantitative data → numerical data that can be counted or measured.

Examples → age, height, income, number of students.

◆ Qualitative → categorical.
◆ Quantitative → numerical.

title: DISCRETE AND CONTINUOUS DATA
notes:
Quantitative data can be divided into discrete and continuous data.

✓ Discrete data → takes separate, countable values.

Examples → number of children, number of books, number of cars.

✓ Continuous data → can take any value within an interval and is usually obtained by measurement.

Examples → height, weight, temperature, time.

◆ Discrete → counted.
◆ Continuous → measured.

title: 7.2 INTRODUCTION TO GROUPED DATA
notes:
✓ Grouped data → data organized into classes or intervals with their corresponding frequencies.

◆ Class interval → a range of values forming one group.
◆ Frequency (f) → number of observations in a class.
◆ Class mark/midpoint (m) → middle value of a class.

Class mark:
m = (lower limit + upper limit)/2

Example:
Class 20–29:
m = (20+29)/2 = 24.5.

→ Grouping makes large data sets easier to summarize and analyze.

title: CLASS BOUNDARIES AND CLASS WIDTH
notes:
◆ Class limits → smallest and largest stated values in a class.

◆ Class boundaries → values separating continuous classes.

For classes 10–19 and 20–29:
Boundaries are 9.5–19.5 and 19.5–29.5.

✓ Class width (i) → difference between consecutive lower boundaries or consecutive upper boundaries.

Example:
10–19 has width 10.

→ Class width is important when drawing histograms and calculating grouped measures.

title: FREQUENCY DISTRIBUTION
notes:
✓ Frequency distribution → a table showing classes and the number of observations belonging to each class.

◆ Frequency → f
◆ Cumulative frequency → cf
◆ Class mark → m

Example:
Class | f | cf
10–19 | 4 | 4
20–29 | 6 | 10
30–39 | 8 | 18

→ Cumulative frequency is obtained by continuously adding frequencies.

4 → 4+6=10 → 10+8=18.

title: 7.3 GRAPHICAL REPRESENTATION OF GROUPED DATA
notes:
✓ Grouped data can be represented graphically to make patterns easier to see.

Main graphs:
1. Histogram
2. Frequency polygon
3. Cumulative frequency curve (ogive)

Different graphs provide different information.

◆ Histogram → frequency distribution.
◆ Frequency polygon → shape and comparison of distributions.
◆ Ogive → cumulative frequencies and locations such as median and quartiles.

title: HISTOGRAM
notes:
✓ Histogram → a graph used to represent the frequency distribution of continuous or grouped data.

◆ Class intervals are placed on the horizontal axis.
◆ Frequencies are represented on the vertical axis.
◆ Rectangles are joined without gaps for continuous data.

Example:
If the class intervals are 10–19, 20–29 and 30–39, each interval is represented by a connected bar.

→ Height of each bar represents frequency when class widths are equal.

title: FREQUENCY POLYGON
notes:
✓ Frequency polygon → a graph obtained by plotting class marks against frequencies and joining the points with straight lines.

◆ Horizontal axis → class marks.
◆ Vertical axis → frequencies.

Example:
For classes 10–19, 20–29, 30–39:
Class marks → 14.5, 24.5, 34.5.

Plot:
(14.5,f₁), (24.5,f₂), (34.5,f₃)

→ Frequency polygons are useful for comparing two or more distributions.

title: OGIVE: CUMULATIVE FREQUENCY CURVE
notes:
✓ Ogive → a graph representing cumulative frequency.

◆ Less-than ogive → uses upper class boundaries and cumulative frequencies.
◆ Greater-than ogive → uses lower class boundaries and descending cumulative frequencies.

An ogive can be used to estimate:
◆ median
◆ quartiles
◆ percentiles.

→ The horizontal axis represents class boundaries and the vertical axis represents cumulative frequency.

title: 7.4 MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY
notes:
✓ Measure of central tendency → a value used to represent the center or typical value of a data set.

Main measures:

◆ Mean → arithmetic average.
◆ Median → middle value when data is arranged in order.
◆ Mode → most frequently occurring value.

Different measures are useful in different situations.

◆ Mean uses every observation.
◆ Median is less affected by extreme values.
◆ Mode identifies the most common value or category.

title: MEAN OF GROUPED DATA
notes:
For grouped data, the exact individual values are unknown, so the class mark is used as a representative value.

✓ Mean:
x̄ = Σfm / Σf

Where:
f → frequency
m → class mark
Σf → total frequency
Σfm → sum of frequency × class mark.

Example:
If Σfm = 1575 and Σf = 100:

x̄ = 1575/100 = 15.75.

→ The grouped mean is an estimate based on class marks.

title: MEDIAN OF GROUPED DATA
notes:
✓ Median → the value that divides ordered data into two equal parts.

For grouped data, first locate the median class containing n/2 observations.

Formula:
Median = Bₗ + [(n/2 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

Where:
◆ Bₗ → lower boundary of median class
◆ n → total frequency
◆ cfᵦ → cumulative frequency before median class
◆ fᶜ → frequency of median class
◆ i → class width.

→ The median class is the class containing the n/2-th observation.

title: QUARTILES, DECILES AND PERCENTILES
notes:
✓ These measures describe the position of observations within a data set.

◆ Quartiles → divide data into 4 equal parts.
Q₁, Q₂, Q₃

◆ Deciles → divide data into 10 equal parts.
D₁, D₂, …, D₉

◆ Percentiles → divide data into 100 equal parts.
P₁, P₂, …, P₉₉

Q₂ = median.
D₅ = median.
P₅₀ = median.

→ For grouped data, locate the appropriate position first, then use the grouped-data formula.

title: GROUPED QUARTILE, DECILE & PERCENTILE FORMULAS
notes:
For grouped data:

◆ Quartile:
Qₖ = Bₗ + [(kn/4 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

◆ Decile:
Dⱼ = Bₗ + [(jn/10 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

◆ Percentile:
Pⱼ = Bₗ + [(jn/100 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

Where:
◆ Bₗ → lower boundary of relevant class
◆ n → total frequency
◆ cfᵦ → cumulative frequency before the class
◆ fᶜ → frequency of the class
◆ i → class width.

title: MODE AND MODAL CLASS
notes:
✓ Mode → the value occurring most frequently.

✓ Modal class → class with the highest frequency.

For grouped data:

Mode = Bₗ + [d₁/(d₁+d₂)] × i

Where:
d₁ = modal frequency − preceding frequency
d₂ = modal frequency − succeeding frequency
i = class width.

Example:
If the class 40–49 has the highest frequency, 40–49 is the modal class.

→ Mode is especially useful for identifying the most common value.

title: INTERPRETING MEAN, MEDIAN AND MODE
notes:
✓ The relationship between mean, median and mode gives information about the shape of a distribution.

◆ Symmetric distribution:
Mean ≈ Median ≈ Mode.

◆ Right-skewed distribution:
Mode < Median < Mean.

◆ Left-skewed distribution:
Mean < Median < Mode.

→ Extreme values strongly affect the mean but usually have less effect on the median.

Therefore, the median is often more appropriate when data contains extreme values.

title: INTERQUARTILE RANGE & POSITION
notes:
✓ Interquartile range (IQR) → spread of the middle 50% of the data.

IQR = Q₃ − Q₁

→ A larger IQR indicates greater spread among the middle half of the data.

Quartiles describe position:
◆ Q₁ → 25% of observations are below it.
◆ Q₂ → 50% are below it.
◆ Q₃ → 75% are below it.

P₈₀ → approximately 80% of observations are below the 80th percentile.

title: UNIT 7 KEY FORMULAS & QUICK REVISION
notes:
◆ Class mark:
m = (lower limit + upper limit)/2

◆ Grouped mean:
x̄ = Σfm/Σf

◆ Grouped median:
Median = Bₗ + [(n/2 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

◆ Quartile:
Qₖ = Bₗ + [(kn/4 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

◆ Decile:
Dⱼ = Bₗ + [(jn/10 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

◆ Percentile:
Pⱼ = Bₗ + [(jn/100 − cfᵦ)/fᶜ] × i

◆ Grouped mode:
Mode = Bₗ + [d₁/(d₁+d₂)] × i

◆ Interquartile range:
IQR = Q₃ − Q₁

◆ Data → information.
◆ Frequency → number of observations.
◆ Histogram → grouped frequency graph.
◆ Frequency polygon → class marks against frequency.
◆ Ogive → cumulative frequency graph.
◆ Mean → average.
◆ Median → middle position.
◆ Mode → most frequent value.
◆ Quartiles/deciles/percentiles → measures of position.
